title: Relational databases
brief: Introduce relational databases through an ordinary application that must keep related facts correct while people read and change them. Establish the model, the work a database performs and the decisions its users remain responsible for. Give an intelligent engineer new to the subject a useful first working model and a route to expert practice in choosing, designing, querying, integrating, diagnosing, operating and recovering a relational service. Keep detailed mechanisms in the contextual articles where they change a practical decision. Make the parent-first reading contract explicit: the current article supplies a usable answer before its contextual children deepen a question. Newcomers finish the working-route parent articles before selecting that depth; readers entering for a particular task see any precise prerequisite section at the contextual entrance.

title: Designing relational data
brief: Teach an engineer to translate application facts, rules and access needs into a relational schema. Follow a booking application from ordinary requirements to tables, identities, relationships, value representations and enforceable rules, exposing the failures each decision prevents. Establish a practical account of normalisation and controlled redundancy, then account for history and deletion. Test the design with representative reads, changes and lifecycle scenarios. Develop specialised modelling only where it changes these relational decisions; leave query fluency, transaction protocols and live migration procedures to their neighbouring articles.

title: Working with SQL
brief: Build practical fluency in reading and writing SQL, from inspecting a disposable database to expressing and checking substantial application and analytical queries. Teach selection, joins, aggregation, subqueries, set operations, window calculations and recursion where they solve useful relational problems. Develop precise reasoning about duplicates, nulls, ordering, time, pagination and data changes. Teach how to establish expected results and test edge cases. Distinguish portable concepts from dialect behaviour without attempting an exhaustive syntax catalogue; leave execution-cost diagnosis to its own branch.

title: Making concurrent changes correct
brief: Teach practitioners to state application invariants, choose transaction boundaries and preserve those invariants under concurrent execution and failures. Connect isolation anomalies to locking, versioned reads, conflict detection, constraints and serialisation, using labelled illustrative schedules and verified engine behaviour. Develop practical choices among atomic statements, conditional changes, locks and stronger isolation, including deadlocks, retries and uncertain commit outcomes. Explain the database's durability boundary and the limit of transactions across external effects; leave detailed client integration and service recovery procedures to their respective articles.

title: Building applications around a relational database
brief: Follow an application request through its driver, connection, statements and transaction to the response and any external effects. Teach how to preserve values and authority at those boundaries, understand the SQL an abstraction performs, bound resource use and recover from failures with evidence about what completed. Build on the transaction article's correctness guarantees; deepen connection management, query composition, request recovery and external work only where their separate decisions need it.

Keep untrusted input out of SQL structure

title: Understanding and improving database performance
brief: Teach a repeatable method for diagnosing relational workloads and making measured improvements. Build the necessary understanding of row and index storage, buffering, version retention, access paths, join methods, sorting, aggregation, statistics and optimiser choices. Read estimated and observed plans without confusing their units or treating estimates as execution evidence. Connect query shape, indexes, physical layout, maintenance and resource contention to workload latency, throughput and capacity. Choose and validate changes with representative data and concurrency, including write and operational costs; deepen engine internals only where they explain a diagnosis or intervention. Give the parent a complete ordinary diagnosis-to-measured-improvement loop. Tell readers to finish this article, including its concluding comparison method, before selecting an optional contextual investigation by the question their evidence raises.

title: Changing a live database
brief: Teach engineers to change schemas, stored data and database locations while applications continue to run. Use a change to an order system to connect application compatibility, physical database work, concurrent writes, verification and recovery. Give every change an explicit sequence, measurable completion conditions and a safe response to interruption. Introduce deeper procedures for schema changes, data jobs and database moves only where they enable reliable relational practice. Treat retention and deletion as changes to the guarantees readers and recovery procedures can rely on. Check concrete procedures against the selected engine, version and deployment.

title: Running a relational service
brief: Teach practitioners to secure, observe, maintain, scale and recover a relational service against explicit availability, data-loss and recovery requirements. Connect those requirements to access boundaries, service signals, capacity, maintenance, topology, backup and incident procedures. Give readers the working model needed to choose a safe next action, with contextual articles developing the procedures and implementation differences. Distinguish self-managed duties from managed service contracts. Keep query tuning, application retry logic and live schema changes in their neighbouring branches, and the separate distributed-systems programme outside this branch.

title: Choosing a relational database
brief: Teach how to select and validate a relational engine and deployment for a concrete application. Turn workload, correctness, latency, availability, locality, operational capacity and total cost into explicit requirements and rejection tests. Compare representative embedded, server and distributed relational choices through the mechanisms that change those tests, including managed service restrictions and responsibilities. Finish with a realistic evaluation and a documented adoption decision. Use neighbouring storage families only to establish suitability; use conditional implementation follow-ups to check a candidate's actual contract. SQLite and CockroachDB are alternative adoption routes, not a required sequence; common disposable PostgreSQL practice starts in Working with SQL before this selection evaluation is complete. Keep the PostgreSQL candidate record here.

title: Choosing types and representing missing values
brief: Choose representations that preserve a value's meaning, allowed states and useful operations across the database and application boundary. Develop a booking schema through prices, identifiers, customer text, reservation times and optional details, using concrete failures to justify each choice. Distinguish exactness from precision, identity from presentation, instants from local schedules, and missing information from empty values. Compare scalar columns, arrays, JSON, binary values, related rows and external payloads through validation, query and ownership requirements. Use selected, documented engine differences only when they change a decision. Leave SQL expression behaviour, constraint design, historical modelling and live migration procedures to their owning articles.

title: Expressing rules with constraints
brief: Teach how to translate application invariants into database constraints and identify what remains outside their scope. Develop a booking schema through required values, candidate keys, tenant-scoped references, conditional uniqueness, mutually dependent rows and non-overlapping reservations. Make each example end with an enforcement decision and valid and invalid changes. Check the selected engine's null, timing and constraint capabilities; reshape the data where that makes a rule enforceable, and state the obligations of triggers or transaction protocols where it does not. Examine update and deletion actions and finish with an enforcement map and concurrency cases for the transactions branch. Leave value representation, transaction anomaly analysis and adding constraints to live data to their owning articles.

title: Normalisation and deliberate redundancy
brief: Teach how to recognise facts with different dependencies, split their storage without losing meaning, and justify retaining a derived copy. Extend the booking design with candidate-key, partial-dependency, transitive-dependency and independent-set cases; introduce normal-form names only when they explain a consequential choice. Check both reconstruction and enforceability after a split. Compare repeated attributes, cached totals, summary tables and materialised results through their read benefit and maintenance contract. Finish with a defensible design and a falsifiable case for its redundancy, using the performance and transaction branches for detailed validation rather than expanding this into a theory or optimisation curriculum.

title: Modelling history and data lifecycles
brief: Teach how to choose among current-state rows, immutable snapshots, change records and effective-dated versions for concrete relational requirements. Distinguish when a fact applied from when the database recorded it, introducing both dimensions only when late information and corrections require them. Design version identity, historical references, interval boundaries and overlap rules so point-in-time questions have a defined answer. Compare status changes, tombstones, archival and deletion through their effects on references, uniqueness, reporting, retention and erasure. Bound the evidence that history rows provide and the removal achieved by deleting live rows; refer operational procedures and live lifecycle changes to their owning branches.

title: Getting SQL values right
brief: Teach practitioners to recognise and repair plausible wrong answers caused by SQL expression semantics. Extend the parent's basic null example through missing-value logic, deliberate defaults, arithmetic, text comparison, conversions and time calculations. Use a compact booking-and-charge report with hand-checked expected values, PostgreSQL as the named reference engine, and documented dialect differences only where they change the result or the repair. Keep representation choices in schema design, aggregate and join semantics in their sibling, membership traps in query composition and driver conversion in application integration. Stop at the depth needed to write and verify ordinary relational queries; no function catalogue or specialist calendar branch is needed.

title: Joining and summarising data
brief: Build correct multi-table application queries and reports by keeping the meaning of one result row explicit. Develop join cardinality, outer-join filtering, grouping, counts, conditional totals and the repair of double-counting with a small connected set of checked examples. Follow the parent-first reading path. Before the first worked task, tell contextual entrants to read Working with SQL's section Express a larger question in checkable stages: its small staged query supplies the derived-table or CTE notation used here. Assume that section alongside the parent's first join and grouped query; concentrate on cases that produce plausible wrong answers. No composition tutorial or prerequisite visit to Composing larger SQL queries is needed. Identify the example engine and consequential dialect behaviour at first use. Keep detailed existence and membership semantics with Composing larger SQL queries, expression semantics with Getting SQL values right, and execution methods and costs with performance. This article supplies the depth needed for expert relational practice without a further reporting or join-specialist branch.

brief: Extend the parent's completed report and existence test with the correctness decisions needed when queries return scalar values, supply tables, compare memberships or combine results. Make cardinality, correlation, null policy, compatible types and duplicate policy explicit. Explain how a checked query becomes a reusable view without implying an execution strategy. Offer one optional hierarchy traversal with deliberate termination, cycle, multiplicity and ordering rules. Use a named engine and identify consequential dialect differences; leave execution costs, materialisation and plan diagnosis to performance, and view deployment to evolution.

title: Calculating across related rows
brief: Teach window calculations as a way to compare and summarise related rows while retaining the required detail. Develop latest rows per entity, top items per group, shares of totals, running and moving totals, and changes from an earlier event using two small, hand-checked datasets. Distinguish input rows, partitions, ordering, peers and frames, and make ties, missing periods and filtering choices observable in expected results. Use a named PostgreSQL version for runnable examples, check consequential behaviour against its primary documentation, and identify dialect differences only when they change a reader's query or result. Assume the parent's basic query and staging workflow; link value semantics, aggregation and execution-cost diagnosis to their existing owners. Stop at reliable application and reporting calculations rather than a function catalogue or analytical specialism.

title: Changing data with SQL
brief: Make INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE express a deliberate change to a known target set, then establish whether their results satisfy the intended postcondition. Extend the parent's first change workflow through set-based changes, insert-from-query, defaults and generated identifiers, constraint failures, ambiguous source matches and conflict-handling choices. Use a small order-and-stock fixture in a named PostgreSQL version, checking consequential behaviour against its primary documentation and recording actual results separately from illustrative examples. Keep conflict-handling inserts, upsert and MERGE together as an outcome decision; identify consequential dialect differences without building a syntax catalogue. Use bounded transactions for disposable exercises and link to transaction reasoning for concurrent correctness, application integration for retries and idempotency, and evolution for production corrections and backfills.

title: Designing changes that coordinate with locks
brief: Teach practitioners to construct and assess explicit locking protocols for relational invariants that ordinary constraints or a conditional row change cannot express. Develop one reservation-capacity example using PostgreSQL at a stated isolation level, with primary-source checks and reproducible sessions required before presenting engine behaviour as established. Cover existing and missing rows, inserts, coordination rows, lock modes, acquisition order, waiting and deadlocks. Finish with an argument covering every writer and a two-session check. Link to isolation for interpreting engine contracts and to application integration for retry machinery; do not expand into a queue or lock catalogue.

title: Reading and testing isolation guarantees
brief: Teach relational practitioners to turn an engine's documented isolation contract and reproducible concurrent sessions into a justified choice of protection and abort handling. Reuse a reservation invariant to trace snapshot visibility, locking reads and concurrent changes, then introduce a staffing invariant only to expose a distinct multirow dependency. Compare PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB only where a verified difference changes the application decision. Distinguish snapshot isolation, serialisability and real-time ordering. Label illustrative schedules separately from observed runs; record engine version, settings, observations and the limited conclusions each run supports. Link to the locking article for protocol construction and to application integration for retry machinery. Stop at the implementation depth needed to use relational transactions correctly.

title: Managing connections and transaction lifetimes
brief: Teach how to own a stateful database connection from acquisition to safe reuse or disposal, including exceptions, cancellation, streaming and shutdown. Separate application handles, pool leases, transactions and database sessions; verify their relationship against the chosen driver and any proxy. Diagnose occupied pools using acquisition wait, lease duration, active database work and connection counts, then bound admission and aggregate connection demand. Extend the parent's ordinary request example through resource failures rather than repeating it. Own cancellation and connection-reuse mechanics here; link to request recovery for deadlines, idempotency and decisions about uncertain operation outcomes, to transactions for correctness guarantees and to performance and operations for workload capacity and service budgets.

title: Controlling the queries your application performs
brief: Make handwritten SQL, query builders and ORM operations accountable for the database work a request performs. Use one bounded order-list example to trace statements, round trips, returned rows and materialised objects; diagnose lazy loading, N+1 reads, joined collection multiplication and implicit writes. Choose projections, loading strategies and batch sizes that preserve the required result while bounding application work. Inspect pagination and streaming at the abstraction boundary, preserve binding and authorisation during composition, and test representative query and result bounds against the selected database and library. Build on the parent's ordinary request and security explanation; leave SQL semantics, physical execution tuning, connection cleanup and request recovery with their existing owners.

title: Recovering database requests safely
brief: Design a bounded application request across pool acquisition, statements, transaction completion and response delivery. Decide what may be repeated from evidence about the database outcome, then give a logical operation a durable identity so overlapping attempts and lost responses can be resolved safely. Keep deadline budgets, retry eligibility, idempotency records and reconciliation within one operation contract. Build on the transaction branch's guarantees; link connection cleanup mechanics and external-effect recovery to their owners.

title: Connecting transactions to background work and events
brief: Make work beyond a relational transaction discoverable and recoverable. Follow one committed order and its external fulfilment request through a transactional job or outbox record, worker ownership, repeated attempts and uncertain external outcomes. Compare direct calls and database change capture by their remaining failure windows. Bound event contracts, ordering, retention and replay to what is needed to account for committed intent; reuse transaction concurrency and request-idempotency mechanisms rather than deriving them again.

title: How stored rows become physical work
brief: Teach the physical model needed to explain page traffic, cache pressure and unreclaimed space in relational workloads. Follow one changing table through reads, wider rows, updates, retained versions and space reuse, connecting each mechanism to evidence and a possible intervention. Use selected PostgreSQL and InnoDB differences only when they change that diagnosis; verify the chosen version's behaviour against primary documentation. Keep row locators here only far enough to understand physical locality; the index article owns traversal, key order, coverage and the detailed secondary-index/base-row access path. Treat physical pruning as one measurable layout intervention. Link transaction semantics and operational reorganisation procedures to their owners, and use the parent's comparison method rather than teaching benchmarking again. Stop at the depth needed for relational engineering decisions, without a separate storage-engine or partitioning curriculum.

title: Choosing indexes for a workload
brief: At the opening, require completion of Understanding and improving database performance, including its concluding Change one explanation into a measured improvement as the common comparison method used here. Derive index candidates from the work a relational workload needs, explain how their keys limit and order access, and decide whether their read benefit earns their write, space and operating costs. Use one tenant order-history workload with equality filters, a date range, an ordered first page and a related-row lookup. Extend it only when another query exposes a consequential trade-off. Supply a compact local reporting legend before using observed index evidence; no sibling article is a prerequisite. Keep the depth at choosing and evaluating relational indexes, without an index-family catalogue or another benchmarking curriculum.

title: Diagnosing a query from its execution plan
brief: Complete one ordinary slow-query investigation in PostgreSQL: collect safe evidence, follow physical rows and repeated work, interpret reporting units, explain a consequential estimate error, test a targeted remedy and accept it against the workload. Use the same reporting query throughout, including common and rare prepared parameters, so statistics and plan choice resolve the original diagnosis rather than begin another tour. Link index design, storage mechanisms, concurrent-load diagnosis and the parent's comparison method to their owners; do not expand into optimiser or storage-engine specialism. No further article is required to finish this task.

title: Changing schemas without breaking applications
brief: Turn an intended schema change into an executable, interruptible procedure with measured limits on production impact. Develop staged constraint validation and a large column-type change, then use a compact operation table to cover related column, index and table changes. Give every stage preconditions, transaction boundaries, completion evidence and a response to failure. Link the data-job and operations owners for their procedures; do not create a separate article for each DDL command or engine.

title: Running reliable data changes
brief: Teach resumable, idempotent data jobs through one backfill that converts the order system's delivery address into a structured representation while orders continue to change. brief: Teach one controlled move of an order database from a source to a destination, following the copy, intervening changes and transfer of write authority. title: Checking a distributed choice with CockroachDB
brief: Decide whether a specific CockroachDB version and deployment meet an application's distributed relational requirements. title: Securing a relational service
brief: Teach how to build and verify operational access boundaries around a relational database, using one service's application, migration, reporting, backup and emergency access tasks. Connect network reachability, identity, privileges, ownership, encryption and audit evidence to what each actor can actually do. Develop safe rotation, revocation and compromise response with selected-engine checks and explicit managed-service responsibilities. Keep application query safety and application authorisation in integration, restoration procedures in backups, and the common incident decision method in service operations. Follow the parent-first reading route through Running a relational service; readers entering here directly should read its section Recover the incident without destroying the evidence before this article's final compromise exercise. This article supplies the operational security depth needed for relational practice; it does not open a general security architecture branch.

title: Monitoring and sizing a relational service
brief: Teach practitioners to establish deployment visibility, maintain capacity and growth budgets, reserve normal and degraded headroom, and act on useful alerts before a service reaches a limit. Produce a dashboard, an evidence-routing table and capacity worksheets tied to service objectives and intervention lead times. Reuse the workload measurement and load evidence from Improving performance under concurrent load (a28), the sole owner of deep concurrent-workload diagnosis. Link to the owning maintenance, topology and restoration procedures for their operational evidence and actions.

title: Maintaining and upgrading a relational service
brief: Teach practitioners to keep a relational service healthy and change its engine version through controlled, observable work. Connect required upkeep to the workload and engine mechanisms that create it; distinguish automatic work, operator intervention and managed-service duties. Build a maintenance and upgrade procedure with explicit resource and interruption budgets, compatibility checks, recovery choices and validation. Use a worked service example and current primary engine documentation for concrete procedures. Link to performance for storage and query mechanisms, to operations neighbours for monitoring, topology and restoration, and to live database changes for schema migration or database moves. Keep this as one practical article.

title: Operating replicas and partitioned data
brief: Choose and operate a relational topology against explicit availability, data-loss, recovery and read-freshness requirements. Follow changes from the writer to a replica, distinguish acknowledgement from replay and usable reads, then practise safe promotion, exclusion of the former writer, reconnection and rejoining. Decide whether local table partitioning preserves the schema and earns its continuing lifecycle cost, then distinguish it from distributing database ownership and assess the routing, transaction, movement and recovery costs of the latter. Use selected-engine and managed-service contracts and bounded failure rehearsals to establish what the deployment can actually deliver. Keep consensus theory, query tuning, application retry mechanics and backup restoration with their owners.

title: Backing up and restoring relational data
brief: Teach relational practitioners to choose recovery copies for named loss cases and prove that they can restore correct data within the required time and loss bounds. Follow one accidental-deletion case from backup selection through an isolated restoration and a controlled return to service, contrasting complete service loss where the procedure changes. Develop consistency, dependencies, retention, independent access, full and point-in-time restoration, selective recovery and measured validation. This is the shared restore procedure used by incidents, database moves and adoption checks; leave incident command, replica promotion, application reconciliation mechanics and migration design to their owners. Check executable procedures against the selected engine and service, and distinguish rehearsed results from intended recovery.
